title: Open Fracture: Protect the Wound, Perfusion, and Infection Risk
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: An open fracture is a contaminated orthopedic emergency. Control bleeding, protect exposed tissue, assess neurovascular status, immobilize, and expedite surgical/antibiotic/tetanus management.
recognize: Bone or deep tissue visible through a wound, severe deformity, bleeding, contamination, or neurovascular compromise.
priorities: ABCs first, then bleeding control, sterile moist/protective dressing as directed, immobilization, distal neurovascular checks, and urgent orthopedic escalation.
assessMonitor: Pain, bleeding, pulses, capillary refill, sensation, movement, skin temperature/color, wound contamination, and systemic stability.
interventions: Do not push protruding bone back into the wound; maintain alignment/immobilization per trauma protocol.
medicationSafety: Antibiotics, analgesia, tetanus vaccine/TIG, and operative prophylaxis are protocol/provider directed.
teaching: Explain need for urgent surgery/infection prevention and repeated circulation checks.
delegationScope: Basic trauma support and repeat neurovascular observations are appropriate; reduction and operative decisions are provider-led.
examTrap: Attempting to reinsert exposed bone into the wound.
oneLinePearl: Open fracture priorities are bleeding, perfusion, contamination control, and rapid orthopedic care.

title: Acute Compartment Syndrome: Escalate Before Pulses Disappear
bottomLine: Pain out of proportion, pain with passive stretch, tense swelling, paresthesia, or progressive neurologic deficit after extremity trauma can indicate acute compartment syndrome. Distal pulses may still be present.
recognize: Escalating analgesic need, severe pain, firm compartment, paresthesia, weakness, or worsening neurovascular findings.
priorities: Notify the surgical team immediately, keep the limb at the ordered position, remove external constriction if authorized, and prepare for fasciotomy evaluation.
assessMonitor: Serial pain, sensation, motor function, capillary refill, pulses, swelling/firmness, and response to interventions.
interventions: Avoid delaying escalation for late signs such as pulselessness.
medicationSafety: Analgesia should not replace serial assessment of worsening pain and neurologic findings.
teaching: Report rapidly increasing pain, numbness, or tightness after fracture/cast placement.
delegationScope: Serial observations may be collected by trained staff; interpretation/escalation requires licensed judgment.
examTrap: Ruling out compartment syndrome because a pulse is present.
oneLinePearl: Pulses can survive while compartments are already ischemic.

title: Pelvic Fracture: Internal Hemorrhage Can Be Massive
bottomLine: Major pelvic fractures can cause life-threatening internal hemorrhage with limited visible blood loss. Hypotension, tachycardia, pallor, abdominal/pelvic pain, or instability requires trauma resuscitation.
recognize: High-energy trauma, pelvic pain/deformity, shock, hematuria, perineal bruising, or neurologic deficits.
priorities: ABCs, hemorrhage control pathway, minimize unnecessary pelvic manipulation, and prepare blood/trauma-team support.
assessMonitor: Hemodynamics, mental status, abdominal/pelvic findings, urine output, bleeding, and distal neurovascular status.
interventions: Use pelvic stabilization/binder only per trauma protocol and correct landmark positioning.
medicationSafety: Analgesia and transfusion follow resuscitation protocol; avoid delaying hemorrhage control for pain treatment alone.
teaching: After stabilization, reinforce mobility and VTE-prevention plans.
delegationScope: Trauma support is team-based; pelvic stabilization and diagnostic decisions are competency/provider directed.
examTrap: Repeatedly compressing the pelvis to check stability.
oneLinePearl: Pelvic trauma can hide a large blood loss.

title: Fat Embolism Syndrome: Respiratory and Neurologic Decline After Long-Bone Trauma
bottomLine: New hypoxemia, respiratory distress, confusion, tachycardia, fever, or petechiae after major long-bone/pelvic trauma can signal fat embolism syndrome and requires urgent escalation.
recognize: Abrupt or progressive respiratory/neurologic changes after fracture fixation or major skeletal injury.
priorities: Assess ABCs/oxygenation, notify the trauma/critical-care team, and support respiratory care.
assessMonitor: SpO2, work of breathing, mental status, temperature, hemodynamics, and ordered imaging/labs.
interventions: Provide oxygen/ventilatory support and maintain fracture stabilization as ordered.
medicationSafety: No routine bedside medication reverses fat emboli; treatment is supportive and provider directed.
teaching: Report new shortness of breath or confusion after major fracture.
delegationScope: Monitoring is appropriate; diagnostic/critical-care management is provider-led.
examTrap: Assuming new confusion is only opioid sedation after a femur fracture.
oneLinePearl: Long-bone trauma plus new hypoxemia or confusion demands embolic deterioration assessment.

title: Suspected Spinal Trauma: Protect Alignment and Watch Breathing/Perfusion
bottomLine: Spinal trauma can threaten cord function, breathing, and blood pressure. Maintain prescribed motion restriction, assess neurologic changes, and escalate respiratory compromise or hypotension promptly.
recognize: Neck/back pain, weakness, numbness, altered sensation, loss of bowel/bladder control, hypotension/bradycardia pattern, or respiratory weakness.
priorities: ABCs with spinal alignment, repeated motor/sensory checks, and trauma-team activation.
assessMonitor: Respiratory effort, BP/HR, motor strength, sensation, pain, bowel/bladder findings, and skin pressure risk.
interventions: Use log-roll/mobility techniques only with trained assistance and the established trauma plan.
medicationSafety: Hemodynamic and analgesic therapy are provider directed; sedatives can obscure neurologic assessment.
teaching: Do not self-mobilize until the spine is cleared/plan established.
delegationScope: Supportive care may be shared; spinal clearance and management are provider/trauma-team responsibilities.
examTrap: Sitting the patient up because pain improved before spinal injury is excluded.
oneLinePearl: Protect alignment until injury is cleared.

title: Hip Fracture in an Older Adult: Pain Control Must Not Hide Delirium and Perfusion Risk
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: Hip fracture can trigger immobility complications, delirium, blood loss, and functional decline. Provide safe analgesia, pressure/VTE prevention, and prompt operative-pathway support while monitoring acute changes.
recognize: Pain with movement, shortened/external-rotated limb, inability to bear weight, or occult fracture after a fall.
priorities: Assess injury and neurovascular status, control pain, prevent further falls/pressure injury, and expedite imaging/orthopedic evaluation.
assessMonitor: Pain, cognition, hemodynamics, skin, mobility, urinary retention/constipation, and medication effects.
interventions: Use prescribed positioning/mobility aids and early multidisciplinary recovery plan.
medicationSafety: Opioids may worsen delirium/respiratory depression; undertreated pain can also worsen delirium—reassess both.
teaching: Reinforce fall prevention, bone health, and postoperative mobility plan.
delegationScope: Routine mobility/skin care may be delegated; acute deterioration and analgesic reassessment require licensed oversight.
examTrap: Attributing all postoperative confusion to age.
oneLinePearl: Hip fracture care is injury care plus delirium, mobility, and complication prevention.

title: Crush Injury: Watch for Rhabdomyolysis and Hyperkalemia
bottomLine: Major muscle crush injury can release potassium and myoglobin, causing dysrhythmia and acute kidney injury. Monitor systemic effects, not just the injured limb.
recognize: Large muscle injury, dark urine, weakness, swelling, oliguria, ECG changes, or shock.
priorities: ABCs, cardiac monitoring when indicated, IV fluid/resuscitation per protocol, and renal/electrolyte surveillance.
assessMonitor: Urine output/color, potassium, CK/renal labs as ordered, rhythm, limb swelling, and compartment signs.
interventions: Maintain perfusion and escalate oliguria, dysrhythmia, or worsening swelling.
teaching: Report dark urine, reduced urine, palpitations, or increasing limb tightness.
delegationScope: Monitoring is appropriate; electrolyte rescue and renal-replacement decisions are provider-led.
examTrap: Treating dark urine as simple dehydration after major muscle trauma.
oneLinePearl: Crushed muscle can become a cardiac and renal emergency.

title: Cast After Trauma: Increasing Pain or Numbness Needs Neurovascular Recheck
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: A cast that becomes increasingly painful, tight, numb, cool, swollen, or associated with reduced movement can signal neurovascular compromise or compartment syndrome. Reassess promptly.
recognize: Pain despite medication, pain with passive stretch, paresthesia, swelling distal to cast, coolness, weakness, or drainage/odor.
priorities: Perform distal neurovascular check and escalate concerning findings immediately.
assessMonitor: Pain, capillary refill, color/temp, sensation, movement, swelling, cast integrity, and skin pressure areas.
interventions: Elevate according to the injury plan and protect cast from pressure/moisture; cast cutting/bivalving is provider/credential dependent.
medicationSafety: Do not simply increase analgesia for unexplained escalating pain without reassessment.
teaching: Report new numbness, blue/cold digits, severe pain, odor, drainage, or wet/damaged cast.
delegationScope: Routine observations may be shared; abnormal neurovascular findings require licensed escalation.
examTrap: Assuming severe pain is expected because the fracture was recent.
oneLinePearl: New pain under a cast is a circulation/nerve question until proven otherwise.

title: Traumatic Amputation: Hemorrhage Control and Limb Preservation Are Parallel Priorities
bottomLine: Traumatic amputation requires immediate hemorrhage control and shock management while the amputated part is preserved correctly for possible replantation evaluation.
recognize: Complete/partial limb loss, major bleeding, shock, contaminated tissue, or associated crush injury.
priorities: ABCs, direct pressure/tourniquet per trauma protocol, IV/blood resuscitation readiness, pain control, and proper part preservation.
assessMonitor: Hemodynamics, bleeding, mental status, residual-limb perfusion/tissue, pain, and associated injuries.
interventions: Wrap amputated part in clean moist material, seal in a bag/container, and cool indirectly per protocol—do not place tissue directly on ice or in water.
medicationSafety: Analgesia, antibiotics, tetanus management, and transfusion are ordered/protocol driven.
teaching: Provide concise trauma-informed explanation and preserve privacy/dignity.
delegationScope: Emergency support is team-based; tourniquet use and part handling follow training/protocol.
examTrap: Putting the amputated part directly on ice.
oneLinePearl: Control bleeding while preserving the part without freezing it.

title: Orthopedic Trauma Reassessment: Trend the Limb, Not Just the Fracture
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Serial neurovascular assessment after fracture, splint, cast, reduction, surgery, or traction detects evolving ischemia or nerve compromise. A change from baseline matters even when pulses remain present.
recognize: Increasing pain, paresthesia, weakness, coolness, pallor/cyanosis, delayed refill, swelling, or altered pulses.
priorities: Compare with prior findings and escalate any meaningful deterioration promptly.
assessMonitor: Pain, sensation, motor function, temperature/color, capillary refill, pulses, swelling, and device tightness/position.
interventions: Maintain prescribed alignment and avoid unapproved repositioning/manipulation of orthopedic devices.
medicationSafety: Analgesia should be paired with reassessment, not used to explain away a worsening limb exam.
teaching: Report new numbness, weakness, color change, or severe increasing pain immediately.
delegationScope: Trained staff may collect neurovascular observations; interpretation/escalation requires licensed judgment.
examTrap: Charting 'pulse present' and ignoring new numbness and weakness.
oneLinePearl: In orthopedic trauma, trend the whole neurovascular exam—not one pulse.
